newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: ALPINE SKIING-DESPITE SUCCESS STROBL REMAINS COOL.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-DESPITE SUCCESS STROBL REMAINS COOL.

text.p: Fritz Strobl has learned the hard way to treat sucess and failure with equal detachment.
Plagued by injury throughout his career, the 24-year-old Austrian has won two downhills this season, including victory on the feared piste at Kitzbuhel on Sunday.
But Strobl remains enviably relaxed in advance of the world championships in Sestriere next week.
"I know what it's like to be at the losing end and it is not a very pleasant place to be," he said in an interview.
"The bad luck and difficulties I had in the past have helped me keep a healthy distance to the sport. I know how quickly and brutally tables can turn.
"I see victories relatively now. Winning is not the most important thing."
Strobl was an up-an-coming youngster when he wrecked his left knee in March 1991 during a Continental Cup downhill in Canada only two months after his World Cup debut in Garmisch-Partenkirchen.
The injury required a complicated operation to repair the torn cruciate and side ligaments as well as the badly damaged miniscus and cartilage.
It kept him off the ski slopes for more than six months and his fight back was hard and uncertain.
"I was only 19 at the time. Far too young to give up and throw all my dreams out the window," said Strobl, whose father, a farmer, taught him how to ski at the age of four.

In December 1992, Strobl returned to the Austrian squad but recurring knee troubles kept him at FIS and Europacup level , with the exception of two World Cup appearances in 1994 in Kitzbuehel and Aspen where he was 20th and 24th respectively.
The turning point in Strobl's career came last winter when he won the overall super-G Europacup to guarantee himself a starting bib in the discipline's World Cup.
Good training results over the summer, after yet another knee operation to remove excess fluid, also put him back into Austria's World Cup downhill team.

Austrian ski federation Alpine director Hans Pum said: "We knew Fritz was an extraordinary talent but he always failed to get good results. We have so many good skiers, we cannot hold on to a skier who can't make the podium.
"We gave him one last chance to prove himself this season and he surprised us all."
Strobl surprised even himself by edging out compatriot Werner Franz by two-hundredths of a second for victory in the winter's first downhill in Val D'Isere.
"Shortly before my start in Val D'Isere, I heard over the loudspeakers that Franz was ahead of (Austrian defending world champion Patrick) Ortlieb.
"I told myself, I can beat these guys in training why shouldn't I be able to beat them in a race? It's unbelievable but I did," he said.
The win also revived memories from 1994, when his compatriot and namesake Josef Strobl also shot to fame with a surprise maiden victory in Val D'Isere. The two men are not related.
Fritz Strobl, a native of Gerlamoos in Austria's southern province of Carinthia, made a further podium appearance when he was third in Wengen, earlier in January.
Despite being Austria's only triumphant downhiller this season, Strobl finds it hard to believe he has qualified for the world championships.
"World championships always seemed so far out of my reach, I never dared to even think about them," he said. "I still don't want to think about them. First I have to see if I have made the team."
But Strobl, who in the past used acupuncture to help him prepare for racing, now adopts a remarkably casual attitude to his sport and is convinced that this is what makes him so strong.
"The secret is that I am not uptight. I stopped thinking about having to win. I just take things in my stride, race by race," he said.
"I consider this winter a gift. Not a gift that was handed to me but one which I earned myself.
"I also made sure I had a life outside ski racing -- I have a job I enjoy as a police corporal and a wonderful girlfriend.
"If I would have been kicked out of the Austrian team this winter, then it wouldn't have been the end of the world."
